1.pericope_label: The generations of Aaron and Moses, and the sons who died

schools.summary: Gill takes the order of the two names for plain seniority and notes how obscure Moses' line is left, unnamed and swallowed up among the Amramites. Calvin observes that Moses only touches here on what he had already told at length, that of four sons two survived, Nadab and Abihu having paid the penalty of their negligence.

Henry reads the recital of the two deaths as a preamble deliberately placed at the head of the law of the priesthood, a warning to all succeeding priests that the holy anointing oil was an honour to the obedient but no shelter to the disobedient, and takes their childlessness for part of the punishment. In the phrase that the survivors ministered in the sight of Aaron he hears that they kept under their father's eye, whereas the two who died had probably got out of it.

Clarke is willing to doubt the text, reporting that some have thought the name of Moses was not originally in the heading and that others resolve the difficulty by rendering the word as acts or history rather than generations; he then turns the silence about Moses' family into an argument for the divine origin of the religion, since a man's invention would have gratified some passion and this one gratified none. Wesley explains the obscurity by the priesthood being given solely to Aaron's posterity, and fixes the chronology, that at Sinai the two sons were still alive though dead when the account was taken.

Ellicott gives the structural reason for Aaron's precedence — his office was perpetuated in his descendants while Moses' ministry was restricted to his own person — and allows the alternative that both were heads of the whole tribe. Keil and Delitzsch read the heading as fixing the Levites' position relative to the priests before a name is counted, and take the note of time as no idle repetition.

debates: Why Aaron is named before Moses. Gill makes it seniority; Wesley makes it the priesthood being Aaron's alone; Ellicott makes it the perpetuation of the office in Aaron's descendants.
Whether the heading is sound. Clarke reports the suggestion that Moses' name did not stand there originally, and the alternative of reading the word as history rather than descent.
outliers: Clarke turns Moses' failure to provide for his own family into an evidential argument, that a religion of human contrivance would have served lust, ambition or avarice, and this one served none though he had it constantly in his power.
themes: Moses provides nothing for his own

5.pericope_label: The Levites given to Aaron, and the charge they keep

schools.summary: Calvin finds two heads here, that the Levites are set apart for the sanctuary and that they act only by the authority of Aaron's house, and presses that the choice was gratuitous lest anyone think himself worthy of it. He then extends the second head well past the text, taking the exalting of one priest as a figure of the one Mediator and turning on those who wrest it into a warrant for setting bishops over presbyters and so for the primacy of Rome; ministers stand under Christ's hand to usurp no dominion. Gill puts the Levites' duty defensively, as securing the sanctuary from being polluted or plundered.

Clarke notes that the verb of presenting is properly a sacrificial word, so that the tribe was given up entirely and was no longer its own but the Lord's property, and describes the Levites as doing the common and laborious offices, taking down, putting up and carrying. Wesley spells out the substitution the charge involves — services due from all the people, which the people could not perform in their own persons, done by particular men in their stead, formerly the firstborn and now these — and defines the intruder as widely as the law does, any man not of Aaron's family though he be a Levite.

Ellicott sets out two senses for the charge and prefers the wider, since the same word is used in the next breath of the congregation. Keil and Delitzsch prefer the servant's posture for the verb, the ordinary expression for standing before a master to receive commands, and keep the duty concrete as the oversight of the furniture, to keep it safe and clean. Both stop at the doubled word given, reading it as emphatic of complete surrender, and both separate these given ones from the later temple servants of foreign descent assigned to the Levites for the lowest duties.

debates: What the Levites were to keep. Ellicott weighs the directions received from Aaron against the charge laid on Aaron and the congregation together, and prefers the second; Wesley and Gill take it the same way, Gill construing it as guard duty over the sanctuary.
outliers: Calvin uses the subordination of the Levites to the priests as an occasion for a polemic against the papacy, arguing that the figure proves the opposite of what it is made to prove — that all ministers stand equally under Christ, who alone succeeds Aaron.
themes: the tribe presented as an offering

11.pericope_label: The Levites taken instead of the firstborn

schools.summary: Calvin puts God's title in terms of purchase, since those whose lives were gratuitously spared in the slaughter of Egypt were bought for himself; having the option of claiming the firstborn of every tribe he was equally free to take a twelfth part from one, which cuts off all handle for complaint. Gill states the sovereignty barely, as an act done of God's own will and pleasure which none should contradict.

Clarke reviews the reasons given for choosing this tribe and finds them inconclusive, preferring the plain consideration that Levi was the smallest tribe and quite enough for the service, a more numerous one being inconvenient; following Ainsworth he carries the type forward to a congregation of the firstborn whose names are written in heaven. Wesley gathers three reasons without choosing — God's respect to Moses and Aaron, a recompence of the tribe's zeal, and its smallness — and explains why the office was concentrated in one tribe rather than left with some men in each, since scattered custodians might have occasioned idolatry, confusion and division.

Keil and Delitzsch trace the chain from the slaying of Egypt's firstborn through the sanctifying of Israel's to this substitution, and note what is gained beyond the exchange itself, a more orderly service from one tribe undividedly devoted to it. Ellicott raises a difficulty in the older command, that its terms do not make clear whether sanctifying the firstborn applied to those then living, which he thinks far the more probable, or was simply prospective.

debates: Why the tribe of Levi. Clarke rejects the zeal at the golden calf as sufficient and settles on the tribe's smallness; Wesley holds three reasons together, including that zeal; Calvin declines the question and rests the choice on sovereignty alone.
Why the firstborn lost the office. Wesley offers forfeiture at the calf or preoccupation with the coming inheritances, without deciding.
themes: one tribe rather than many hands

14.pericope_label: Numbered from a month old, and the three sons of Levi

schools.summary: Calvin makes the counting of infants an act of fairness rather than of piety: had God taken only those past twenty it could not have been known how many firstborn there were and the compensation would have been uncertain, so the indulgence should have made the people readier to pay for the shortfall. On the three names he reflects that twelve men grew in so short a time into so many thousands, which shows how powerfully God works under the semblance of weakness, and refers Kohath's promotion to the same gratuitous good pleasure that called Moses. Gill notes only that the tribe was left out of the general muster and counted apart, for a different purpose.

Henry states the contrast with the other tribes — twenty years old and able to go to war against a month old and upward — and makes the surplus his point, since little more than a third of these were ever fit for the service and God would have them all numbered as retainers of his family, that none should think himself disowned for not being in a capacity to serve. He adds the descent rule, reckoning after the house of the fathers and not the mothers, and looks ahead to the three hundred by which the family figures overshoot the total, supposing those struck off were firstborn Levites already sanctified and so unable to enter the exchange.

Clarke argues the month-old rule from arithmetic, since numbered from twenty they would not have come near the firstborn of the twelve tribes, and since those were of all ages their substitutes had to be. He also notices who did the counting and finds a delicacy in it: Moses numbered the Levites alone though he and Aaron together numbered the twelve tribes, because the redemption money was to be paid to Aaron and it was not decent that the man who profited by a surplus should take the number himself. Wesley gives the reason from the other end, that a month was when the firstborn were offered, and notes the different ages at which Levites are numbered for other purposes.
Ellicott notes that the same age governs the firstborn themselves and was afterwards fixed as the age of redemption.

debates: Why the Levites were numbered from a month old. Clarke argues from the need to match firstborn of all ages; Calvin from the need to know the shortfall exactly; Wesley and Ellicott from the age at which the firstborn were offered and later redeemed; Henry from a principle about who belongs to God's household.
outliers: Clarke's observation that Moses numbered this tribe alone, so that the party who stood to gain by an excess did not take the count, is a point of procedural propriety none of the others raise.
themes: Moses seeks nothing for his own line

21.pericope_label: Gershon: families, number, station, chief and charge

schools.summary: Gill names the two families from the first son of Levi and glosses the chief as the man having authority over them and the direction of what they were to do.

Clarke stops at the number and doubts it, suggesting the figure may originally have read two hundred rather than five hundred, two Hebrew letters being easily confounded — a conjecture he will need again when the totals fail to agree. Wesley divides the charge by simple exclusion, the tabernacle here meaning not the boards, which belonged to Merari, but the ten curtains; the tent meaning the curtains of goats' hair; the coverings the skins above them; and the cords those by which the whole was fastened to the pins and stretched out.

Keil and Delitzsch give the tally and place the house under Eliasaph on the western side. Ellicott lays out the whole encampment at once, priests east, Kohathites south, Gershonites west, Merarites north, and then works closely on the vocabulary: the tent and the tabernacle are not the same thing, the second being the wooden building with its curtains and the first the covering over it; the hanging at the entrance was of blue and purple and scarlet and fine twined linen; the word rendered door means an opening rather than a door, though at Shiloh the sanctuary later had doors. On the cords he corrects the natural reading, since the court's cords belonged to the Merarites.

debates: Whether the Gershonite total is sound. Clarke proposes a scribal confusion of two Hebrew letters giving seven thousand two hundred for seven thousand five hundred, which would resolve the chapter's arithmetic.

27.pericope_label: Kohath: the favoured house, and Eleazar over all

schools.summary: Gill weighs the numbers before accepting the compliment: eight thousand six hundred was the largest of the three houses, but with twice as many families as either of the others the increase was not so large in proportion. He reads the encampment forward into what happens later in the book, since this house pitched between the tabernacle and the camp of Reuben, which is how Korah the Kohathite came to be intimately acquainted with Dathan and Abiram the Reubenites; and he finds a second motive in the chief named here, Elizaphan being of the youngest of the four families, so that some have thought Korah's dissatisfaction began at seeing a younger house preferred.

Wesley lists the privileges of the house together — Moses and Aaron and all the priests out of it, the chief place, the care of the most holy things, and twenty-three cities in Canaan, almost as many as both their brethren received — and then repeats the point the chapter keeps making, that the posterity of Moses were not distinguished from other Levites at all. He fixes Eleazar's rank as next under the high priest, performing his work in his absence, and identifies the hanging in their charge as the one covering the most holy place.

Ellicott draws the consequence of the descent of Moses and Aaron from Kohath, that this house received the most honourable portion of the service and that Eleazar was set over the whole body of the Levites, and supplies the philology of the southern station, the Hebrew name for the south being taken from the word for the right hand. Keil and Delitzsch list the charge as the ark, the table, the candlestick, the altars and the vessels, and describe Eleazar's office by the word used for it, a superiority over the chiefs of the three families.

outliers: Gill alone uses the camp plan as historical explanation, deriving the alliance of Korah with Dathan and Abiram from the fact that the Kohathites pitched next to Reuben.
themes: the house of Moses and Aaron
the right hand of the camp

33.pericope_label: Merari: the frame of the sanctuary

schools.summary: Gill names the two families from Merari's sons and explains why this house alone needed help: the boards were the walls of the holy and the most holy place, and because they and what went with them made a heavy carriage the Merarites were allowed waggons, and more of them than the Gershonites, while the Kohathites had none. One phrase he will not take as it stands, holding that the chief of the house of the father of the families should rather be rendered the chief of the house, the father to the families — the common father of them all — so that the title states an office rather than tracing a descent.

Keil and Delitzsch set the tally under Zuriel on the northern side and describe the duty as a cycle rather than a custody: to take the boards, bars, pillars and sockets in charge when the dwelling was taken down, to carry them on the march, and to fix them again when it was set up. Ellicott adds a cross-reference to the description of the court and its pillars given in Exodus.

debates: How the chief's title should be rendered. Gill prefers to read it as naming the man father to the families rather than son of a father of them, which turns a genealogical note into a statement of office.

38.pericope_label: The priests on the east, and a total that will not add up

schools.summary: Gill notes simply that the entrance was on the east, so that Moses and Aaron and Aaron's sons lay across the way in.

Clarke's conjecture at the Gershonite figure, that two easily confounded Hebrew letters have turned two hundred into five hundred, is a solution of the same shape as Keil and Delitzsch's but applied at the other end of the list. Wesley offers two readings of the priests' charge and declines to choose, since they may have kept it in the people's stead or for the people's benefit and preservation.

Keil and Delitzsch state the discrepancy without softening it — the three houses come to twenty-two thousand three hundred and the muster is recorded as twenty-two thousand — and show that the smaller figure must be the true one, since the whole later transaction depends on the firstborn exceeding the Levites by exactly two hundred and seventy-three. They consider the rabbinic reconciliation and reject it as forced and unsatisfactory, on the ground that an account this circumstantial would not have omitted such a fact, and propose instead a copyist's error in the Kohathite number. Ellicott examines the word for sanctuary and finds it of wider compass than either the word for the wooden dwelling or the word for the tent, taking in the court as well.

debates: How twenty-two thousand three hundred becomes twenty-two thousand. Keil and Delitzsch weigh the traditional answer, that three hundred Levite firstborn were already sanctified and could not be exchanged, reject it as forced, and posit a copyist's error in the Kohathite figure; Clarke posits the same kind of error in the Gershonite figure instead. Both agree the recorded total is the sound number.
themes: the fourth side of the square

40.pericope_label: The firstborn numbered, and twenty-two thousand two hundred and seventy-three

schools.summary: Gill reports the rabbinic answer he finds in Jarchi and Abarbinel and in the Talmud, that the surplus was settled by lot — twenty-two thousand slips written for a Levite and two hundred and seventy-three written for five shekels, mixed and drawn — and mentions that some supposed the money was paid from a public stock instead, which was a ready way of doing it though whether reasonable is less clear, since the firstborn were the property of particular persons.

Henry reports a stricter version of the counting rule from bishop Patrick, that none were numbered but those born since the coming out of Egypt, and then follows it somewhere unexpected: if all of them were born in that single year, there must have been an abundance of marriages in the last and bitterest year of the servitude, by people who were not discouraged by the present distress but married in faith. That the two numbers come out so near each other he takes for a mark of providence rather than coincidence.

Clarke works out the redemption in his own currency and then attacks the rabbinic lot outright, calling it a most stupid and silly tale that no intelligent people could have resorted to, and holding it much more likely the charge was met from a general fund. Wesley supposes instead that the exchange began with the eldest of the firstborn and worked downward, so that the two hundred and seventy-three redeemed with money were the youngest.

Keil and Delitzsch set out the mechanics, twenty-two thousand exchanged for the Levites and the cattle set against the firstlings without being matched head for head. Ellicott treats the figure as a serious difficulty rather than a comfort, since against six hundred thousand males of twenty and upward it yields roughly one firstborn to forty-four, which has been urged as a ground for rejecting the narrative; he answers first that a writer producing so many complicated calculations would hardly insert one so improbable, and then offers two solutions, restricting the firstborn to those under twenty not already counted, or extending the term to the firstborn of every household including the children of concubines and slaves.

debates: How the two hundred and seventy-three were identified. Gill reports the rabbinic lot without endorsing it; Clarke calls that tale silly and prefers a general fund; Henry and Wesley suppose the exchange ran from the eldest downward, leaving the youngest to be redeemed.
Whether the number of firstborn is credible. Ellicott states the objection at its strongest and answers it two ways; the other witnesses take the figure as given.
themes: marriages in the years of bondage

44.pericope_label: Five shekels a head, and the money given to Aaron

schools.summary: Calvin states the principle before the sum: since the complete portion of God was not found in the tribe, it had to be supplied from elsewhere, and he supplies what the reader needs to know what was paid, that the shekel of the sanctuary was the double shekel worth two of the ordinary kind. Gill converts the price into his own currency and notes it became the settled rate afterwards; he is candid that the text does not say of whom the money was exacted, children of a month old being unable to pay and their parents paying for them, and he ends on the man who handled it, observing that Moses converted none of it to his own use.

Wesley guards the clause about the cattle from a misreading: they were not taken from the Levites nor sacrificed, any more than the Levites themselves were, but presented before the Lord by way of acknowledgment, the beasts remaining with the men for their support in God's work.

Ellicott points to where the standard shekel is first defined and observes that the law of redeeming the firstborn at five shekels came into operation from this moment; he is equally frank that the manner of determining the families is unrecorded, and offers the two guesses open to him, the most recently born or the lot. On the cattle he notices there appears to have been no numbering at all, and that the whole of the Levites' herd was given for all the firstlings of all the other tribes. He then denies what the arrangement is usually taken to prove, holding that a priesthood of the firstborn transferred to the Levites is altogether without foundation, since the patriarchal priesthood belonged to the head of every family, was exercised before the command to sanctify the firstborn was given, and was thenceforth confined to Aaron's family not as substitutes for the firstborn but in the place of the whole nation.

outliers: Ellicott's three-part denial that the Levites inherited a priesthood of the firstborn cuts against the reading the rest of the chapter's expositors assume, and is the sharpest dissent in the chapter.
themes: what the substitution did not transfer
